transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, to be honest, I just... I really don't feel like myself anymore. I mean, I used to be able to at least get through the day and have a normal conversation, you know? But lately, I barely talk to people. I just go completely flat and quiet. It's like the volume gets turned all the way down inside my head and I can't find the dial to turn it back up. 

I work as a building cleaner, doing the evening shifts mostly, and usually, it's just me and my supplies. But lately... just getting started on the cleaning route feels like pushing a loaded cart uphill in the mud. I'll just stand there in the janitor's closet, looking at the mop bucket and the industrial cleaner, and I can't even muster the energy to mix it with the water. It’s this heaviness. And when someone does walk by, like one of the late-night office workers, I used to say hello, ask about their evening, maybe talk about the news or something—I took some college classes back in the day, so I always liked to keep up with things and chat. But now? I just stare. I don't have the words. I just feel so incredibly empty and flat, like all the air has been let out of my tires. 

It takes absolutely everything out of me just to put one foot in front of the other down those long, empty hallways. The whole night just stretches out in front of me, and I can't bring myself to care or to speak or to even move half the time. So, I guess that's why I'm here. Because pushing that heavy cart uphill every single night when I feel this hollowed out... it's just getting to be too much to handle on my own.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it hasn't been a sudden thing, you know? It's more like a slow leak. I'd say it's been building up for about... oh, a year and five months now. Yeah, a year and five months. It all started right around the time I had to move out of my old apartment. I'd lived in that neighborhood for years. I knew the guy at the corner store, I knew the mail carrier's schedule, I knew which streetlights flickered on Elm Street. It was my routine, my home base. But then the rent went up, and the building got sold to some development company, and they basically pushed everyone out so they could renovate and charge double. 

So, I had to pack up everything—which is a whole ordeal in itself when you're my age and you've accumulated a lifetime of boxes you never unpack—and move across town to a place that just doesn't feel right. I don't know my neighbors here. The walls are thin, but somehow I feel more isolated than ever. And ever since that move, ever since I lost my footing in that old neighborhood... that's when this heaviness started creeping in. At first, I thought I was just tired from the packing and the stress of finding a new place on a janitor's salary, which isn't exactly easy, let me tell you. But the tiredness never went away. It just turned into this... this flat, empty feeling. It's like leaving that apartment left a hole in me, and for the last year and a half, it's just been getting wider and deeper, until now I'm just standing in front of my mop bucket staring at the wall.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

Well... no. No, I really don't. And that's... that's part of what makes it all so incredibly heavy, you know? Because I used to have things that I looked forward to. I wasn't just a guy pushing a mop. I had my little routines that brought me some peace. Like... Saturdays. Saturdays used to be my day. I'd wake up early, before the sun was even fully up, and I'd head down to the lake with my tackle box. I've been fishing since I was a boy—my grandfather taught me how to tie a proper knot when I was maybe seven or eight—and there was just something so... so calming about watching the water, feeling the line, waiting for that little tug. I didn't even care if I caught anything half the time, it was just the ritual of it. 

And then, on Sunday mornings, it was the crossword puzzle. I'd make a pot of strong coffee, sit at my little kitchen table—the one I had in my old apartment, right by the window where the morning light came in—and I'd work through the Sunday paper. I always did it in pen, too, which I was pretty proud of. And even at work, I used to get a kick out of showing the younger guys the ropes. You know, these kids come in, they think they know everything, but they don't know the first thing about properly stripping and waxing a linoleum floor without leaving streaks. I used to actually enjoy taking them aside, showing them the right technique, the right pressure to apply. It felt good to pass that on.

But now? Now... I don't know. The fishing rods are just gathering dust in the corner of my new place. I look at them, and I just think about the effort it would take to load the car, drive to the lake, bait the hook... and for what? I don't feel that calm anymore. I don't feel anything. The crossword puzzles just look like a jumble of meaningless boxes, and the coffee just tastes bitter. And at work, when a new guy comes on shift, I just let him make a mess of the floors. I don't say a word. I just watch him struggle, and I don't even care enough to step in. I just let all those things sit there—the fishing, the puzzles, the teaching—because I try to do them, or I think about doing them, and they just... they don't give me anything back anymore. It's like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in the bottom. You pour and you pour, but it just stays empty.
Have you ever thought about not wanting to live or had thoughts of suicide during this time?

Well... that’s... that’s a heavy question, isn't it? I guess... I mean, to be completely honest with you, and it's hard to say this, but... yes. Yes, I have. 

Now, I want to be clear right off the bat, I don't have some big plan. I'm not sitting in my apartment figuring out how to do something drastic, I'm not hoarding pills or anything like that. I've always been a practical guy, and honestly, like I said before, I barely have the energy to mix floor cleaner these days, let alone plan out something like ending it all. 

But... it’s the mornings. Well, my mornings, anyway, since I work the evening shift. I wake up in that new bedroom—the one where the window just faces a dirty brick wall instead of the street like my old place, where I used to be able to watch the neighborhood wake up—and I hear my alarm buzzing. And I just lie there staring at the ceiling. And a lot of mornings... a lot of mornings I wake up thinking it might just be easier if I didn't wake up at all. If I could have just slipped away in my sleep and stayed in the dark where it's quiet, where I don't have to face the empty hallways or the heavy cart or just... the sheer effort of existing for another twenty-four hours. Just the thought of having to put my feet on the floor feels impossible, like I'm wearing lead boots.

And I'll tell you, having that thought... realizing that I genuinely wouldn't mind if my life just quietly stopped... it scares me. It really does. It scares me enough to actually say it out loud to you right now, which isn't something I ever thought I'd do. You know, a man my age, you're supposed to just push through, have some grit, keep your chin up. My grandfather, the one who taught me to fish, he used to say you just put your head down and do the work. But when that first thought hits you before you've even thrown off the blankets, just wishing the world would go away permanently... it's terrifying. It really is. Because it happens so often now, just lying there, listening to the neighbor's TV through the thin walls, wishing I just wasn't here anymore.
Have you noticed any changes in your movement or activity level, such as feeling restless or having trouble sitting still?

Restless? No... no, I wouldn't say that. If anything, it’s, well, it's the exact opposite of that. I don't have any of that nervous energy, you know? You see some folks, maybe some of the guys I work with in the maintenance crew, they drink three or four cups of that terrible breakroom coffee and they're tapping their feet, pacing around the supply closet, just can't stay in one spot for two minutes. But me? I don't have that at all. Like I was saying before about the heaviness... it really settles into my bones. 

I have this old recliner in my new living room—it's this faded green corduroy thing I’ve had since maybe '98, dragged it all the way from the old apartment, which was a nightmare to get up the stairs here—and I can just sink into that chair and not move a muscle for hours. I don't even turn the television on most of the time. I just sit there. The thought of getting up, even just to walk the ten feet to the kitchen sink for a glass of tap water, it feels like I'd be trying to walk through wet cement. 

So, no, pacing around or feeling antsy... that's not me. Even pushing the cart down the hallway at work, I used to have a pretty good clip to my step, especially back in my younger days when I was taking some night classes at the community college and always hustling from the bus stop to the campus and then to my shift. I was always on the move back then. But now, I just feel glued to the floor. Sitting still is just about the only thing I *can* do without it feeling like a monumental chore. Honestly, I could probably sit still all day if nobody made me get up.
Have you lost any weight over the past year and a half?

Well, you know, it's funny you should ask that, because I was just noticing something about my uniform the other day. I've been wearing the same style of work pants for... oh, it's got to be fifteen years now. Dickies, navy blue, the ones with the reinforced knees because of all the bending and kneeling you have to do when you're scrubbing baseboards or fixing a leaky trap under a sink. Anyway, I always buy them a little snug around the waist because they stretch out, but lately... lately I've had to pull my belt in by at least two notches. Maybe three. They're just hanging off me, really. 

And it's not because I'm trying to lose weight or anything like that. I've never been one for diets or counting calories or whatever it is folks do. It's just... I don't know, my appetite is just gone. Completely gone. I'll open the fridge when I get home from my shift—usually around midnight, when the building is finally quiet and the last of the office workers have gone home—and I'll just stare at the shelves. I used to make myself a decent sandwich, maybe some turkey and Swiss on rye with a little bit of mustard, maybe heat up some soup if it was cold out. I always liked a good bowl of split pea soup. But now? Most days, food just tastes like cardboard. There's no flavor, no enjoyment in it whatsoever. It's just another chore, like everything else.

So a lot of times, I just skip meals altogether. I'll go the whole day on just that bitter coffee I mentioned, maybe a glass of water. Or if my stomach starts really gnawing at me, I'll just grab a handful of saltine crackers from the pantry and eat those standing over the sink before I go to bed. Just enough to stop the rumbling so I can try to get some sleep. But an actual, proper meal? Sitting down with a plate of hot food? I can't even remember the last time I had the desire to do that. It's just too much effort for something that brings me no satisfaction anyway. So, yeah, I'd say I've definitely lost some weight. I don't own a scale, but the way those work pants are fitting, it's pretty obvious.
Do you find it difficult to initiate activities or do you feel like you're moving in slow motion most of the time?

Well, yes, that’s exactly it. That’s actually a big part of what brought me in here to talk to you in the first place, because I just don’t feel like myself anymore. Getting started on anything... it’s just a monumental task. 

Take my job, for instance. Getting started on my cleaning route every evening, it literally feels like I’m pushing a loaded cart uphill. And I mean a really loaded cart. You know those big grey utility carts we use? The ones with the heavy-duty casters? Normally you've got your mop bucket, your wringer, the yellow wet floor signs, all the industrial spray bottles hanging off the sides, maybe three or four heavy bags of wet trash. It's a heavy rig on a good day. But lately, just the thought of grabbing the handle of that cart and pushing it out of the basement supply closet... it feels like the wheels are locked and I'm trying to shove it up a steep hill in the mud. I'll just stand there in the closet with my hand on the plastic handle for... I don't know, ten, fifteen minutes sometimes, just trying to will my legs to take that very first step. Everything is just in slow motion. 

And it's not just the physical movement, either. It’s... I don't know how to explain it, but it's like my whole personality is in slow motion, too. I barely talk to people anymore. I just go completely flat and quiet. There’s this security guard, Frank, who works the front desk at the main building I clean. Good guy, maybe a few years older than me. We used to shoot the breeze every single night when I clocked in, talk about the baseball scores or how terrible the city traffic was getting, just normal everyday stuff. But now? Now I just kind of look at him. My face just feels... blank. Heavy. Like the muscles in my face just gave up and I can't even force a smile. 

Frank will ask me how I'm doing, and I just kind of stare at him, and my mind is just empty. I don't have the words anymore. I just mumble something and shuffle past him toward the elevators. It's like the part of my brain that comes up with things to say or cares about having a conversation just completely shut down. So yeah, I'm moving slow, but I'm also just... I'm just flat. I'm not me anymore. Just dragging myself through the shift, pushing that imaginary weight... it takes everything I have just to get the wheels rolling.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things that have happened?

Well... yeah. Yeah, I do. It’s actually... it weighs on me constantly, this feeling like I’ve just let everyone down. I just keep thinking about how I failed everybody by losing my old place. I mentioned that old apartment earlier, the one I had to drag that green recliner out of... I lived there for a long time, and I just couldn't keep it going. I couldn't keep my life together, and I ended up having to pack up whatever I could fit in a borrowed van and leave. I just sit in that chair now, and my mind just spins and spins, telling me how I messed it all up, how I should have been able to hold onto it, how I'm just a massive disappointment. It’s this heavy, sinking feeling right in the middle of my chest that I’m just a complete failure. 

And the strange thing is, doctor, it doesn’t even stop with the things that are actually my fault. It bleeds into everything else, things I don't even have any real control over. Like... well, there's this church a few blocks from my new place. Sometimes I hear they're running low on donations for their food drive, you know, the church pantry is short on supplies, canned goods, that sort of thing. And I'll sit there in my living room and genuinely feel like it's my fault. Like, if I had just kept my life together, maybe I could have helped them, or somehow I’m directly to blame for those shelves being empty and people going hungry. It makes no logical sense, I know I don't run the church, but the guilt... the guilt is just as real as if I'd stolen the food myself. 

Or at work... say one of the guys on the day shift calls out sick and a hallway gets missed on the third floor. Now, I only clean the ground floor and the basement, like I said. I don't even take my cart up past the lobby. But if I hear that a hallway got missed and somebody complained about scuff marks or tracked-in mud, I feel this horrible pit in my stomach, like somehow that’s on me, too. Like I should have known, I should have gone up there and checked, I should have fixed it before anyone noticed. I just take the blame for the whole world falling apart, and I don't know how to turn it off. It just makes that heavy feeling I was telling you about so much worse.
Have you ever experienced any unusual thoughts or heard voices that others couldn't hear?

Well... it's strange you ask that, because... I didn't really know how to bring this up, and honestly, it makes me feel like I’m losing my grip even more than I already am. But, yes. Yes, I have been hearing something. 

You know how I was telling you about my cleaning route, how I work the late shift? Usually, by the time I get around to doing the wet mopping on the ground floor—I use this big, wide-loop cotton mop, the heavy industrial kind that really soaks up the water and the floor cleaner—the building is just completely dead. I mean, you could hear a pin drop in those hallways after midnight. Even the air conditioning hum kind of dials back. It’s just me and the squeak of my work boots on the linoleum. 

But lately, when I’m mopping after hours, making my figure eights back and forth, I’ll hear a voice. It’s a man’s voice. Deep, kind of echoing just a little bit. And he’ll just say my name. Clear as a bell, like he's trying to get my attention. Or sometimes, it’s not my name, sometimes he’ll say, "You missed a spot right there." 

And I’ll stop dead in my tracks, you know, my hands gripping the mop handle, and I’ll look right over toward the main stairwell. Because that’s exactly where the voice is coming from. It sounds clear as day, like he is standing right there by those heavy metal fire doors at the bottom of the stairs, just watching me work. The first few times it happened, I figured it was Frank, the security guard I mentioned, maybe doing his late-night rounds, or maybe one of the office managers who stayed way past midnight and decided to take the stairs instead of the elevator. 

So I'll call out. I'll say, "Frank? That you?" or I'll say, "I'll get that spot right now, sorry about that." And I’ll walk over there, pushing the wet floor sign out of the way, and I'll pull open that heavy stairwell door expecting to see somebody standing on the landing. But... there’s nobody there. Absolutely nobody. Just the empty concrete stairs going all the way up to the second floor. I'll even lean over the railing and look up, thinking maybe they walked away real fast, but there's no sound of footsteps, no doors clicking shut. Nothing. 

But I know I heard it. It’s not just the pipes clanking in the walls or the wind outside, I know what those sound like, I've worked in buildings my whole life. This is a real person's voice, speaking right to me, telling me I missed a spot when there isn't a single living soul in that hallway but me. It just... it really shakes me up, doctor. I just stand there staring at the empty stairs, feeling that heavy feeling in my chest get even heavier, wondering if my mind is finally just breaking down completely on top of everything else.
Do you ever feel like you're fidgeting or can't sit still when you're not working?

Well, no... no, not at all, doctor. It’s actually the complete opposite of that. Like I was trying to explain earlier with how heavy everything feels, how I'm just dragging that imaginary weight around... when I’m not on the clock, I barely move at all. 

You remember that green recliner I mentioned? The one I managed to salvage from my old place before I had to pack up the van? When I get back to my new apartment after a shift, usually around maybe two or two-thirty in the morning depending on how the night bus is running... I just sit down in that chair. And I mean, I really just sit. I don't tap my foot, I don't wring my hands, I don't bounce my knee or pace the floor or anything like that. I don't even take my work boots off right away most nights. I just sink into those cushions and it's like I'm glued to the upholstery. The thought of getting up to even walk the ten feet to the kitchen sink for a glass of tap water just feels completely impossible. 

So there's definitely no restless energy, no fidgeting. It's more like whatever energy a normal person has just drained right out through the soles of my boots. Sometimes I'll just sit there in the quiet, watching the light from the streetlamp outside shining through the living room blinds, just watching the dust motes float in the air, and suddenly I'll realize the sun is coming up and I haven't moved a single muscle in four or five hours. Just sitting there, heavy as a block of concrete, while my mind spins with all those guilty thoughts I was telling you about. So, no, I don't have any trouble sitting still. Sitting still is... well, it's about the only thing I feel capable of doing anymore.
How long have you been having these thoughts about not wanting to live?

How long... well, it’s hard to put an exact day on it, doctor. It kind of just creeps up on you, you know? Like dust settling in a corner, you don't really notice it until it's just coating absolutely everything. I'd say it's been building up for a while now, maybe the last couple of months, especially since I had to pack up and move into this new place and everything just felt like it was completely falling apart on me. 

I want to be clear about this, because I know how it sounds and I don't want you to think I'm... well, I don’t have some big plan. I’m not sitting alone in my apartment mapping out how to, you know, how to end it all. I don't have anything hidden away in the medicine cabinet, I haven't bought anything, I'm not making preparations or anything like that. Honestly, like I was saying before about having absolutely no energy and just sinking into that green recliner for hours on end, I don't think I'd even have the physical strength to put a plan together right now if I tried. 

But... the truth is, a lot of mornings, I'll open my eyes—usually the sun is just starting to come through those cheap plastic blinds in my bedroom, and I can hear the early morning traffic starting up out on the street—and I just feel this immediate, crushing disappointment. I just wake up thinking it might be easier if I just didn’t wake up at all. If I could have just stayed asleep forever, you know? Just slipped away in the night. Because then I wouldn't have to get up and feel that heavy, sinking weight in my chest, I wouldn't have to worry about letting everyone down or taking the blame for the whole world, I wouldn't have to go push that heavy cotton mop in the middle of the night and hear that man's voice echoing out of the stairwell. It would just be quiet. 

And I'll just lie there on my mattress, staring up at the water stains on the ceiling, just wishing I could fade away into nothing. But then... then this cold feeling kind of washes over me. Because realizing that I actually want that, realizing that I'm actively wishing to just not exist anymore... it really scares me. It scares me enough to actually sit here in this chair and say it out loud to you today. Because I don't know what to do with these thoughts, doctor. They just sit there in my head, morning after morning, telling me everything would be easier if I was gone, and it's just terrifying to feel like I'm starting to agree with them.
Do you think the voice you hear is real or just a product of your mind?

That’s... see, that’s the million-dollar question, isn't it? And honestly, doctor, I just... I don't know. I really don't know. I've been wrestling with that exact question every single night since this started. 

Because... well, logically, right? I went to college for a couple of years back in the day, I know how to think things through. Logically, I know the building is locked up tight. I know the security protocols, I know who has the keys, I know the alarm system is armed on all the perimeter doors. So, by all the facts on the ground, there is absolutely no one else in that hallway with me. Which means... which means it has to be just my mind playing tricks on me, right? It has to be a product of my own head, especially with how run down and heavy and guilty I've been feeling lately. My brain must just be misfiring under all that weight.

But then... but then I'm actually standing there. And I hear it. And it's not like a thought. You know what a thought feels like, it’s inside your head, it doesn't have a... a physical location in the room. But this voice... when he says my name, or tells me I missed a spot, I can hear the sound waves actually bouncing off the cinderblock walls in the stairwell. I can hear the slight acoustic echo it makes when it hits the long stretch of linoleum floor. It has direction, you know? Like, it sounds like it's coming from exactly fifteen feet away, slightly to my left, right next to the red fire extinguisher cabinet on the wall. 

How can my brain invent an echo? How can my mind make a sound that actually feels like it's vibrating the air outside of my ears? I've worked in empty commercial buildings my whole adult life, I know exactly how sound travels in them. And this sounds like a real, physical person speaking into the space. 

So I'll just stand there, gripping the mop, just staring at that heavy metal door, and I feel like I'm being split right down the middle. Half of me is terrified that there really is some guy standing in the shadows watching me work, maybe someone who slipped past the cameras or hid in a closet before lockup, and the other half of me is even more terrified that my mind is just completely broken and manufacturing things out of thin air. I'll spend the next two hours of my shift just going over and over it, pacing my route, trying to convince myself it was just the HVAC system or the pipes, but... I don't know. I just really don't know what to believe anymore. It feels as real as you and me talking right now, but I know it can't be. It just can't be.
How often do you have these thoughts about not wanting to live?

Well, like I was trying to explain just a little bit ago when we were talking about it... it’s a lot of mornings. Almost every single morning now, if I really stop and think about it. It didn't start out that way, you know. At first, it was maybe just once a week, usually on a Tuesday or a Wednesday when the work week just stretches out ahead of you and you can't see the end of it. But now? Now it's pretty much every time I open my eyes. 

I really want to make sure you understand, though, because I know we circled back to this, and I want to be clear—I don't have some big plan. I really don't. I'm not trying to figure out a way to make it happen, I don't have the energy for a plan anyway, like I said. But it's just... it's just that heavy, awful feeling that hits me the second the alarm goes off or the sun comes through the blinds. A lot of mornings, practically all of them lately, I just wake up thinking it might be easier if I just didn’t wake up at all. If I could have just stayed asleep and never had to face the day. 

And having that exact same thought every single day, having it become just a normal part of my morning routine right alongside putting on my work boots and making a cup of instant coffee... that’s what really gets to me. It scares me enough to say it out loud to you today, because having it happen this often, day after day... I just don't want to get so used to the thought that I stop being scared of it, you know? If it happens every day, what if I just accept it? So, to answer your question about how often... it's a lot. Most days. Almost every day now.
Have you had any periods where your symptoms improved or went away completely since they started a year and a half ago?

Well... a year and a half... it feels like ten years, honestly. But, to answer your question about things going away... there was this one stretch. Just one, really. It lasted for maybe... I don't know, several weeks? I remember thinking maybe I was finally turning a corner, because that heavy, awful feeling we were just talking about, it actually lifted some. I wasn't waking up with that immediate dread quite as bad. I was actually getting through my meals, sitting down at the kitchen table and eating a proper plate of food instead of just staring at it, and getting through my shift at work felt a little smoother, like I wasn't dragging my boots through wet cement the whole night. 

But the thing is... and this is what really confuses me, doctor... even though my mood was better, and I had a little more energy to just get through the day, the other stuff didn't go away. Not at all. I’d still be out there on my shift, feeling okay physically, but I still heard that voice calling my name in the stairwell. Exactly the same as before, echoing off the linoleum. 

And... I don't know if I've mentioned this part yet, but the security cameras out in the main hallway... even when I was feeling better, I stayed completely convinced they were being used to track me. I'd walk past them with my cart, see that little red light on the dome, and I just knew, I knew in my gut that someone was sitting in a room somewhere logging every single step I took, watching me, tracking my whole route through the building. 

So... I guess you could say some things improved for a few weeks, the sadness and the energy part, but the voice and the cameras... those never stopped. They were right there with me the whole time, even when I was having a good day.
Have your symptoms gotten worse since they first started a year and a half ago?

Worse? Yeah... yeah, I'd say they have. And you know, you keep saying a year and a half, but if I'm being perfectly exact about it, if I really sit down and look at the calendar, it's been building for about one year and five months. I know the exact timeline because... well, I know exactly what kicked all this off. It’s been building up ever since I had to leave my old apartment and my old neighborhood.

I lived in that place for a long, long time, doctor. It wasn't anything fancy, just a little one-bedroom walk-up, but it was mine, you know? I knew the whole neighborhood. I knew the guy at the corner store, I knew the bus routes by heart, I knew exactly how the radiator clanked in the winter. It was my anchor. It was safe. But then the building got sold to some big management company out of state, they jacked up the rent, and they basically priced me right out of my own home. I had to pack up my entire life into boxes. And moving at my age, trying to find a new place I could afford on a building cleaner's wages, dealing with all those deposits and the physical hauling... it takes a heavy, heavy toll on a person. 

So ever since I had to leave that apartment, ever since I lost that neighborhood... that's when this all started. And it didn't just hit me all at once on moving day, no. Like I said, it’s been building. It’s like... you ever see a slow leak in a pipe at work? First it's just a drop, just feeling a little down about the move, missing my old routine. But then the drops keep coming, and the pressure builds up behind the wall, and the sadness gets heavier and heavier, and then the cameras start feeling like they're watching me, and the voice starts up in the stairwell... It just kept piling on, month after month, getting a little worse, a little more intense, ever since I handed over those keys one year and five months ago. I just... I haven't had a solid piece of ground to stand on since I left that neighborhood, and everything has just been snowballing from there.
Have you experienced any other unusual perceptions or thoughts besides the voice in the stairwell?

Well, besides the voice at work... yeah. Yes, there is something else. And it actually goes right back to that new apartment building I was just telling you about. I know I mentioned the security cameras at my job earlier, but... well, it’s happening at my new place, too, and honestly, it’s even worse there because that's where I'm supposed to be resting. 

At the new building, I just... I get completely stuck on this idea. I can't shake it, no matter how much I try to rationalize it or push it out of my head. I get stuck on the fact that the new landlord, along with a couple of the other people who live on my floor... I just know they're keeping tabs on me. They use the hallway cameras to do it. I'll be coming home from a long shift, my feet are aching, and I'll walk down that hall and I just know they're watching the feed. And it's not just watching, it's... they're passing messages about me. I'll see those two specific tenants in the hall, or I'll hear them murmuring right as I pass by the camera lens, and it's like they're coordinating. Logging when I come and go, sharing it with the landlord, passing these little messages back and forth about what I'm doing. 

And the thing is, I've tried to talk about it. I've tried to reason it out. And folks tell me—the maintenance guy there, some of the other neighbors—they swear up and down that those cameras are just for the front door. They tell me over and over, they say it's just to see who buzzes in, it's just standard security for the lobby and it doesn't even point at my door.
